This means the abstract strategy interface is coupled to a specific GitHub implementation type, preventing genuine platform-agnostic strategy implementations and contributing to an import cycle in the rulesets/ directory.

review::.::holistic::abstraction_fitness.summary: 22 interfaces with only a single implementation each

evidence: src/sync/types.ts defines 10+ interfaces (lines 1-424). The review packet identifies 22 one-impl interfaces and 75 indirection hotspots. RepositoryProcessor's constructor accepts 9 optional component overrides via these interfaces, but tests are the only consumer of overrides.
detail.suggestion: The codebase has 22 interfaces that each have exactly one implementing class: IFileWriter/FileWriter, IManifestManager/ManifestManager, IBranchManager/BranchManager, IAuthOptionsBuilder/AuthOptionsBuilder, IRepositorySession/RepositorySession, ICommitPushManager/CommitPushManager, IFileSyncOrchestrator/FileSyncOrchestrator, IPRMergeHandler/PRMergeHandler, ISyncWorkflow/SyncWorkflow, IRepositoryProcessor/RepositoryProcessor, and others. While some enable test mocking, the sheer count (22) creates indirection without demonstrated benefit, inflating the codebase with type declarations that mirror their sole implementation.

review::.::holistic::abstraction_fitness.summary: AuthenticatedGitOps uses reflection to access private GitOps internals

evidence: Line 86: `const internal = gitOps as unknown as GitOpsInternal;` accesses private properties workDir and execGit. The class also has 12 local operation pass-through methods that simply delegate to this.gitOps without adding behavior.
detail.suggestion: AuthenticatedGitOps casts its wrapped GitOps instance to an internal type to access private properties: `const internal = gitOps as unknown as GitOpsInternal`. This bypasses TypeScript's type system and couples AuthenticatedGitOps to GitOps implementation details. If GitOps internal property names change, this breaks silently at runtime.

review::.::holistic::error_consistency::.summary: Mixed error strategies across modules without clear convention

evidence: validator.ts throws errors directly. ProcessorResult has success/message fields. sync-command.ts wraps processor.process() in try/catch (line 305-347) even though process() returns result objects with success:false rather than throwing. Settings processors return {success: false, message} on error but are also wrapped in try/catch by sync-command.ts.
detail.suggestion: The config/ module uses thrown errors for validation failures. The sync/ module uses result objects (ProcessorResult with success/message fields). The settings/ processors use result objects but also wrap everything in try/catch returning error results. The CLI layer (sync-command.ts) adds its own try/catch around processor calls that already return error results. There is no documented convention governing which approach to use where.
